details:
**Lobster Trap and Fish Tail**
Calder's 1939 mobile commissioned for the stairwell of the Museum of Modern Art in New York. It is made of painted steel wire and aluminum sheet fins, with a wire "trap" and red-painted shapes suggesting the title sea creatures, all hanging from balanced rods that move with air currents. It is the most common title clue for him.

**Mobiles and stabiles**
Calder invented the mobile, a hanging kinetic sculpture of weighted shapes balanced on wires and rods that move with air currents or motors; Marcel Duchamp coined the name "mobile" for his works in 1931. His stationary abstract sculptures, by contrast, are called "stabiles," a term suggested by Jean Arp.

**Flamingo**
Calder's 53-foot-tall red steel stabile in Chicago's Federal Plaza, in front of the Kluczynski Federal Building, unveiled in 1974. Its tall arching "legs" and a "head" that touches the ground suggest the title bird, and its bright color makes it stand out from the surrounding dark office buildings.

**Mercury Fountain**
Calder's fountain for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the 1937 Paris World's Fair, displayed alongside Picasso's Guernica. It commemorates the Republicans' defense of the mercury mines at Almadén against Francisco Franco's forces during the Spanish Civil War; liquid mercury flows over metal plates beneath a hanging red disk, and the toxic work is now kept behind glass at the Fundació Joan Miró in Barcelona.

**Cirque Calder (Calder's Circus)**
A portable miniature circus Calder built in Paris in the late 1920s from wire, wood, cloth, cork, buttons, and other household materials. Its figures include acrobats, sword swallowers, lion tamers, contortionists, and a trapeze set, and Calder narrated and moved them himself in live performances; it is now at the Whitney Museum, along with related wire works such as Two Acrobats.

**Calder red**
The signature bright red-orange paint Calder used on many of his large outdoor sculptures, including Flamingo, La Grande Vitesse, Eagle, and Bent Propeller.

**La Grande Vitesse**
Calder's large red stabile in Grand Rapids, Michigan, installed in 1969 as the first public artwork funded by the National Endowment for the Arts. An abstraction of it appears in the city's official logo.

**Eagle**
A large red steel stabile by Calder that now stands in the Olympic Sculpture Park of the Seattle Art Museum.

**Mountains and Clouds**
Calder's monumental work for the atrium of the Hart Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., which combines a black steel "mountain" stabile on the floor with a "cloud" mobile hanging from the ceiling. It was installed in 1986, a decade after his death. His final large mobile, a 76-foot-long work, hangs in the East Building of the National Gallery of Art.

**Bent Propeller**
A red Calder stabile that stood at the World Trade Center in New York and was destroyed in the September 11, 2001 attacks.

**A Universe**
A 1934 motorized Calder work at MoMA in which red and white spheres, suggesting planets, move along wire paths, completing a full cycle in about forty minutes. A separate motorized wall work, Universe, hangs in the lobby of Chicago's Willis (Sears) Tower.

**Acoustic Ceiling (Floating Clouds)**
Calder's installation of large colored panels suspended from the ceiling of the Aula Magna auditorium at the Central University of Venezuela in Caracas. Designed with acoustic engineers, the "clouds" both decorate the space and improve its acoustics.

**Constellations**
A series of abstract wood-and-wire sculptures Calder made during World War II, when metal was scarce. They share their title with the Constellations series of gouaches by his friend Joan Miró.

**Man (Trois disques)**
A huge stainless steel stabile Calder created for Expo 67 in Montreal, with legs digging into the ground and peaks that end in three disks.

**Animal Sketching and the National Police Gazette**
Before becoming a sculptor, Calder trained as a mechanical engineer at the Stevens Institute of Technology and worked as an illustrator for the National Police Gazette, sketching prizefights and the circus. His 1926 book Animal Sketching collected brush and ink drawings from the Bronx and Central Park Zoos.
